text: INFORMS defines predictive analytics at the analytics-type level as providing insight into what will happen in the future.
For model-building practice, predictive analytics uses historical/current observations with statistical or machine-learning models to estimate an unknown or future outcome for new cases.
Outputs may be classes, probabilities, numeric values, rankings, risk scores, or forecasts.
The practical requirement is generalization: performance must hold on data not used to fit or select the model.

text: Predictive models exploit statistical associations that improve estimation of an outcome.
A variable can be highly predictive without being a cause of the outcome.
Prediction asks: “What outcome is likely for this case?” Causal inference asks: “How would the outcome change if we intervened?”
This distinction becomes essential when a prediction is converted into a treatment, offer, policy, or other action.

text: Time-Series Forecasting: Time Changes the Validation Rules
Forecasting estimates future observations of a variable indexed through time.
Model choice depends on forecast horizon and temporal structure such as level, trend, seasonality, autocorrelation, and structural change.
Naive and seasonal-naive forecasts are essential benchmarks because a complex model must beat a credible simple forecast.
Future-known regressors (for example, scheduled promotions) may be used; information unavailable at forecast time must not leak into evaluation.
Forecast validation must preserve temporal order and evaluate the horizons used operationally.
Moving Average: A Smoother and Simple Forecasting Device
A k-period moving average replaces the current level with the arithmetic mean of the most recent k observations.
Larger windows smooth more strongly but respond more slowly to change.
Moving averages are useful for smoothing and can serve as simple short-horizon forecasting baselines in appropriate series.
They do not, by themselves, explicitly model trend, seasonality, causal drivers, or changing variance.

text: Model Families Are Candidates, Not Winners
A model family should be considered because its assumptions and strengths fit the scenario—not because it won another dataset.
Model complexity should earn its place by producing materially better decision-relevant performance.
Transparent baselines remain valuable even when a more complex model is selected.
The final comparison must use the same validation folds/time windows, preprocessing logic, and decision-relevant metrics.
The phrase “best model” is incomplete until you state: best for which target, metric, horizon, cost structure, and deployment setting?

Converts score/probability into Positive vs Negative
Precision, Recall, Specificity, F1/F-beta at the chosen threshold
Choose using consequences, capacity, and policy — not automatically 0.50

TPR versus FPR; AUC summarizes ranking
Useful general ranking summary; can look optimistic when positives are very rare
Precision versus Recall; Average Precision summarizes PR performance
Often more informative for strongly imbalanced positive classes
Whether stated probabilities match observed frequencies
A predicted 0.80 should correspond to roughly 80% observed positives in comparable groups
Useful when probabilities feed expected value, risk, pricing, or optimization; not measures of calibration alone

Forecast Accuracy Metrics — Keep Time, Scale, and Baseline in View
Forecast error with extra weight on large misses
Undefined/infinite at zero; unstable near zero; requires a meaningful ratio-scale zero
Absolute error scaled by naive / seasonal-naive training error
Scaling benchmark must match seasonality; MASE < 1 indicates lower average absolute error than the scaling benchmark
Positive and negative errors can cancel
Forecast Accuracy Metrics — Keep Time, Scale, and Baseline in View
Forecast Evaluation Must Match the Decision Horizon
Evaluate on future observations that were not used to fit the model; in-sample residuals are not a substitute for genuine forecast errors.
Preserve time order. Use rolling-origin / time-series cross-validation so each forecast is trained only on information available before that forecast origin.
Score the horizons that matter operationally (for example, 1-week, 4-week, and 8-week ahead) instead of averaging away horizon-specific weakness.
Always compare against a simple benchmark such as naive or seasonal-naive forecasting before claiming improvement.
When the decision depends on uncertainty, evaluate interval, quantile, or distributional forecasts in addition to point forecasts.
One Practical Decision Map for Evaluation Metric Selection
Binary action at a fixed threshold
Precision, Recall, Specificity, F-beta; explicit cost
Are the top-ranked cases useful within capacity?
Can the probability be used quantitatively?
Do typical errors or large misses matter more?
MAE vs RMSE; R2 only as supporting context
At what horizon and scale is error costly?
Start with the prediction product, then choose the metric that represents how the prediction will be used.
Evaluation Metrics — The Rules That Matter
There is no universally best evaluation metric. “Best” depends on the prediction product, error consequences, and downstream decision.
Choose the metric before final model comparison whenever possible; otherwise it is easy to optimize whichever score makes the preferred model look best.
Compare candidate models under the same validation / resampling design so the comparison is fair.
Report complementary measures when one score hides a relevant trade-off: Precision + Recall, discrimination + calibration, MAE + Bias, or point accuracy + uncertainty.
For classification, model selection and threshold selection are related but separate decisions.
Translate scores into operational consequences: missed cases, false alerts, review load, pesos of error, service level, or expected loss.
Choosing the Best Predictive Model per Scenario
There Is No Universally Best Predictive Model
Predictive performance is necessary but not sufficient.
Scenario fit includes target type, data volume/structure, nonlinearities, imbalance, probability quality, interpretability, latency, retraining burden, and error consequences.
A simpler model may be preferable when performance is comparable and explanation, speed, stability, or governance matters.
A more complex model should win only when its incremental value survives realistic validation and operational constraints.

text: Start with the Business Decision, Then Define the Prediction
How much inventory should be positioned?
Which offer is most likely to convert?
Treatment/response model; causal method if effect is claimed
Step 1 — Define the Target, Horizon, and Label
Target: What exactly will count as success/event/value?
Horizon: How far into the future must the prediction remain useful?
Unit: customer, transaction, branch, product-day, shipment, patient, etc.
Label timing: Is the outcome observed after the feature window, or are we accidentally including future information?
Actionability: Will the prediction arrive early enough for an intervention?
Step 2 — Match Candidate Models to the Data Regime
Step 3 — Define the Cost of Errors Before Picking the Winner
For classification, quantify or at least rank the harm of false positives and false negatives.
For regression/forecasting, ask whether underprediction and overprediction have different costs.
For ranked queues, define review/intervention capacity: top 100? top 1,000? all above a threshold?
If possible, convert model errors into expected business cost or net benefit rather than treating metric points as inherently valuable.
A 1-point gain in accuracy may be irrelevant; preventing 50 costly misses may be decisive.
Step 4 — Decide How Much Interpretability Is Required
Transparent models or reliable local explanations
Coefficients, tree structure, global importance + diagnostics
More complex model may be acceptable
Latency: Does the prediction need to arrive in milliseconds, minutes, daily, or monthly?
Feature availability: Will every required predictor exist at the exact prediction moment?
Infrastructure: Can the organization host, score, monitor, and retrain the model reliably?
Stability: Will small changes in data cause disruptive changes in decisions?
Cost: Is the incremental performance worth compute, licensing, engineering, and maintenance?
Step 6 — Decide Whether You Need Ranking, Class Labels, or Reliable Probabilities
Step 7 — Prevent Data Leakage with a Pipeline Mindset
Data leakage occurs when information unavailable at prediction time influences model building or evaluation.
Split data before learning preprocessing quantities; fit imputation, scaling, feature selection, encoding, and other learned transformations only from training data within each validation split.
For temporal problems, future observations must not influence earlier features, model selection, or preprocessing.
Ask of every feature: “Would this value truly be known when the prediction is made?”
Use reproducible pipelines so cross-validation applies transformations only to the appropriate training portion.
Leakage produces overly optimistic evaluation and commonly collapses when the system meets truly new data.
Candidate Model Scorecard: Strengths by Scenario
Transparent baseline; probability or numeric prediction
Local similarity on scaled low-dimensional data
CV over K + relevant class/regression metric
Decision: retention team can contact only 2,000 customers per week.
Target: churn within 30 days; features must be available before the contact decision.
Candidate models: Logistic Regression as transparent baseline; Decision Tree / Random Forest / Gradient Boosting for nonlinear interactions.
Primary evaluation: precision and recall within the top 2,000 or at the operational threshold; check calibration if probabilities drive offer cost.
Winner: not necessarily the highest-AUC model—choose the model that finds enough true churners within team capacity at acceptable false-contact cost.
Decision: order inventory today for the next eight weeks.
Compare seasonal-naive baseline, Moving Average / exponential smoothing, ARIMA-type model, and ML/regression with promotions/calendar if those future inputs are known.
Use rolling-origin validation and compare error at horizons 1 through 8.
Use MAE when average unit miss is central; RMSE when severe stockout/overstock misses deserve extra penalty; MASE for scaled comparison across products.
Reject models that use future promotions or stockout-censored demand incorrectly.
Fraud is often rare, so ordinary accuracy can be dominated by legitimate transactions.
Decision: which transactions should be passed, challenged, manually reviewed, or blocked?
Use the precision-recall curve and Average Precision for rare-event ranking comparison; then inspect precision/recall at the actual review threshold or queue capacity.
If expected financial loss uses predicted probabilities, inspect calibration and proper probability scores.
A multi-band policy may be better than one threshold: auto-block very high risk, review intermediate risk, pass low risk.
Choose only if extra recall creates enough value
The “best” model depends on the value of incremental recall versus calibration, explanation, latency, and maintenance—not on a single leaderboard number.
Predictive Model Selection Framework — Scenario First
1. Define the business decision and who/what is being predicted.
2. Define target, prediction horizon, unit of analysis, and prediction moment.
4. Select several model families whose assumptions/capabilities fit the data structure.
5. Define the costly errors and choose decision-aligned metrics before comparison.
6. Use realistic validation and prevent leakage; for time series, preserve temporal order.
7. Compare generalization, calibration when needed, interpretability, stability, latency, and maintenance.
8. Select the operating threshold / queue capacity / forecast policy.
9. Confirm on untouched test data and important subgroups.
10. Deploy only when incremental decision value justifies complexity; monitor live outcomes.
“Best model” means best validated model-policy combination for this scenario—not highest score in the abstract.

EDA is an approach, not another analytics type.It helps us understand what the data reveals through distributions, patterns, anomalies, relationships, and emerging hypotheses. Descriptive, Diagnostic, Predictive, and Prescriptive Analytics describe the purpose of the analysis

EDA discovers the clue; Diagnostic Analytics investigates the clue.EDA can reveal an unusual pattern, but diagnosis asks where it is concentrated, when it began, who or what is affected, which factors move with it, and what explanations remain plausible.

Diagnostic Analytics asks “Why did it happen?” without turning “why” into guesswork.Diagnosis systematically localizes an observed outcome, investigates relationships and contributing factors, and develops evidence-supported explanations.
Localization comes before explanation.Drill-down and decomposition help identify where the change lives and what contributed to it before analysts attempt to explain the underlying mechanism.

Association is diagnostic evidence, not automatic causation.Relationships, statistical tests, residuals, and candidate drivers can narrow the explanation space, but stronger evidence is required before claiming that one factor caused another.

For categorical diagnosis, use the chain: EXPECT → TEST → LOCALIZE → MEASURE STRENGTH.Expected Frequency establishes the independence reference; Pearson Chi-Square tests overall association; Pearson Residuals identify where the discrepancy is concentrated; Cramér’s V measures association strength.

Time can be diagnostic without being predictive.Time-series decomposition separates historical observations into trend, seasonal, and residual components so analysts can distinguish recurring structure from unusual variation. Forecasting begins when the question is what happens next.

A diagnostic visualization must support investigation, not decoration.The right visualization should make comparisons, concentration, contributions, process losses, anomalies, relationships, or temporal changes easier to investigate and trace.

Diagnostic Analytics is now increasingly AI-assisted, but not AI-autonomous.AI can detect anomalies, suggest drivers, recommend drill paths, etc., but analysts remain responsible for validating the data, comparisons, context, alternatives, and causal claims.
